questions.subtopic: 1B1 Acting with integrity. Pressure to drop a finding
questions.question: A seafood plant manager asks internal auditor Marek to drop a significant finding on missed cold-storage checks from the draft, because repairs have started. Which response BEST shows honesty and professional courage?

options.A: Drop the finding now that repairs are closing the gap
options.B: Raise the finding at the closing meeting and leave it unwritten
options.C: Keep the finding and acknowledge the repairs already under way
options.D: Keep the finding and refuse to discuss it further with the manager

questions.key_concept: A significant finding is never left out; action management has started is acknowledged beside it, not used as a reason to drop it.
questions.pre_read: Separate two things: what the evidence showed, and what management has done about it since.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.1 Honesty and Professional Courage forbids hiding or leaving out a finding, and Standard 15.1 Final Engagement Communication has the internal auditor acknowledge action that management has already begun. So the finding stays, with the repairs noted beside it. Raising it only by word of mouth is the runner-up: the manager hears it, but the written communication that others rely on would still be incomplete.

wrong_explanations.A: Repairs change what happens next, not what the evidence showed. A significant risk has to be written up and reported as a finding; the repairs are acknowledged with it.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the manager is told, but a significant finding kept out of the written communication is still an omission that its other readers never see.
wrong_explanations.D: Professional courage is truthful, respectful communication. Internal auditors still discuss a disagreement with management and listen for a valid reason to change the results.

tips: Eliminate: A, because started repairs do not erase what the evidence showed, and D, because courage is truthful and respectful, not a refusal to talk.
Final two: C beats B because a significant finding belongs in the written communication; telling the manager aloud still leaves it out for every other reader.
Exam cue: when management has started fixing a problem, CIA answers usually keep the finding and acknowledge the action. A fix under way is not a reason to omit.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Acting with integrity. Ethics concern outside the scope
questions.question: Auditing fuel inventory at an airport, internal auditor Oksana sees buyers accept supplier gifts that the code of conduct forbids; procurement is outside the engagement scope. Which action is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Report the concern as the organization's ethics policy directs
options.B: Set the matter aside as outside the approved engagement scope
options.C: Record it in the workpapers for the next procurement engagement
options.D: Report the buyers to the national anti-corruption agency

questions.key_concept: Conduct that breaks the organization's ethical expectations is reported as policy directs, whether or not it sits inside the engagement scope.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the duty to speak up depends on what this engagement was set up to cover.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.2 Organization's Ethical Expectations requires an internal auditor who identifies conduct that breaks the organization's ethical expectations to raise the concern by the route its policies and procedures set. The duty is not tied to the engagement scope. Saving the matter for the next procurement engagement is the runner-up: it preserves what was seen, but nobody with authority learns of it and the conduct continues.

wrong_explanations.B: The reporting duty in Standard 1.2 covers any such conduct the auditor identifies in the organization. The scope limits the testing, not the duty to report.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a workpaper note preserves the facts, but the concern reaches nobody able to act. Reporting under the policy is required now, not at a later engagement.
wrong_explanations.D: Concerns go first through the route that policy and law set. An outside disclosure is made when a law or regulation requires one, which the facts do not show.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the duty to report is not limited by the engagement scope, and D, because an outside disclosure follows the routes policy and law set.
Final two: A beats C because reporting under the policy is a requirement now; a note for a later engagement tells nobody with authority to act.
Exam cue: when an internal auditor notices misconduct outside the engagement scope, CIA answers usually report it through the organization's own channel, without waiting.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Acting with integrity. Tolerated legal violation
questions.question: Internal auditor Kofi finds a gold refinery understating export weights, breaking customs law; the director says executives tolerate it, and policy sends suspected violations to the compliance officer. What should Kofi do FIRST?

options.A: Treat the practice as a risk that management has accepted
options.B: Notify the customs authority before anyone inside is alerted
options.C: Hold the matter for the final engagement communication
options.D: Report the facts promptly to the company's compliance officer

questions.key_concept: A legal violation is reported to those with authority to act, by the route law and policy set, even when management tolerates it.
questions.pre_read: Notice who already knows about the practice, and what the organization's own policy says about suspected violations.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.3 Legal and Ethical Behavior requires an internal auditor who identifies a legal violation to report it to people with authority to act, as laws, regulations and policies specify. Here the policy names the compliance officer. Executive tolerance changes nothing: overlooking tolerated illegal activity is itself discreditable. Waiting for the final engagement communication is the runner-up, but it leaves a continuing violation unreported for weeks.

wrong_explanations.A: Tolerance by executives does not lift the duty in Standard 1.3 to report a legal violation. Overlooking illegal activity the organization tolerates is itself discreditable conduct.
wrong_explanations.B: Reports go to parties with authority to act as laws, regulations and policies specify. An outside disclosure is made when the law requires it; here policy sets the route.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the finding does belong in that communication, but the duty to report a legal violation by the policy route does not wait for the engagement to end.

tips: Eliminate: A, because executive tolerance does not cancel the duty to report a legal violation, and B, because the route is the one law and policy specify.
Final two: D beats C because the policy route applies as soon as the violation is identified; the final communication may be weeks away.
Exam cue: when management says a violation is known and tolerated, CIA answers usually still report it, through the channel that policy and law name.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. Objectivity or independence
questions.question: A courier's internal audit function reports directly to the board, yet a supervisor finds internal auditor Akinyi rated a depot control effective mainly because its manager is a close friend. Which conclusion is MOST accurate?

options.A: The function's independence is impaired despite its reporting line
options.B: The auditor's objectivity is impaired despite the reporting line
options.C: The reporting line shows that the auditor's rating was unbiased
options.D: A friendship without money involved creates no impairment

questions.key_concept: Independence belongs to the internal audit function and comes from its position; objectivity is each internal auditor's own unbiased mindset.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose problem this is: the function's place in the organization, or one person's judgment.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.1 Individual Objectivity requires each internal auditor to keep an impartial, unbiased mindset, and Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity requires them to avoid conflicts of interest, which a close friendship can create. The problem sits with one person's judgment. Calling it an independence impairment is the runner-up, but independence describes the function's position, which the direct reporting line to the board already supports.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: something is impaired, but independence is the function's freedom from conditions that bias its work. The board reporting line is intact; one auditor's judgment is not.
wrong_explanations.C: A sound reporting line supports objectivity but cannot supply it. Each internal auditor must still keep an unbiased mindset on every engagement.
wrong_explanations.D: Conflicts of interest include personal relationships and favoritism, not just financial ties. The test is whether judgment could be influenced, or appear to be.

tips: Eliminate: C, because board reporting supports objectivity but cannot prove one auditor is unbiased, and D, because relationships count as conflicts, with or without money.
Final two: B beats A because the bias sits in one auditor's judgment; independence is about the function's position, which is sound here.
Exam cue: function and reporting line point to independence; one person's bias, relationship or past role points to objectivity.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. Recent former responsibility
questions.question: Internal auditor Meera managed a lender's collections unit until seven months ago and disclosed this to the chief audit executive. Which assessment of Meera leading an assurance engagement on collections is MOST accurate?

options.A: Disclosing the former role has restored Meera's objectivity
options.B: Objectivity is presumed impaired for this assurance work
options.C: The function's independence is impaired by Meera's earlier transfer
options.D: Objectivity is unaffected now that Meera has left the unit

questions.key_concept: For assurance over an activity an internal auditor was responsible for in the past 12 months, objectivity is presumed impaired; disclosure does not lift that.
questions.pre_read: Check two facts first: is the engagement assurance or advisory, and how long ago did the responsibility end?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity tells internal auditors to refrain from assessing an activity they used to be responsible for, and for assurance work it presumes objectivity is impaired when that responsibility ended in the past 12 months. Seven months is inside the window. Relying on the disclosure is the runner-up, but disclosure to the requesting party is the condition for advisory work, not a cure for assurance.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: disclosure is required, and it is the condition for advisory work on a former responsibility. For assurance inside 12 months the presumption of impairment remains.
wrong_explanations.C: Independence concerns the function's position and reporting line. A past job held by one internal auditor is a question of that person's objectivity.
wrong_explanations.D: Leaving the unit does not remove the pull of judging one's own earlier decisions. The presumption runs for 12 months after the responsibility ended.

tips: Eliminate: C, because one auditor's past role is an objectivity matter, not the function's independence, and D, because the presumption lasts 12 months after the role ended.
Final two: B beats A because disclosure clears advisory work, not assurance; inside 12 months, objectivity is still presumed impaired.
Exam cue: former responsibility plus assurance plus under 12 months means presumed impaired. Look for the option that keeps that auditor off the assessment.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. Spotting a conflict of interest
questions.question: A chief audit executive is staffing an assurance engagement on grant awards at a regional arts fund. Which internal auditor's circumstance MOST clearly creates a conflict of interest?

options.A: Audited the same grants process two years ago
options.B: Worked for another arts funder before joining the organization
options.C: Met the grants manager at professional training events
options.D: Serves unpaid on the board of a current applicant

questions.key_concept: A conflict of interest is a competing personal or professional interest; an unpaid role with a party the engagement affects counts, in fact or appearance.
questions.pre_read: For each circumstance, ask what the auditor personally stands to gain, lose or protect from the engagement's results.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity requires internal auditors to avoid conflicts of interest: a competing personal or professional interest that could sway judgment, or appear to. A board seat with a current applicant gives the auditor a stake in who wins grants, paid or not. Having audited the process before is the runner-up: it can breed familiarity bias, which must be managed, but it is no competing interest.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: repeat audits can dull skepticism, a bias the auditor must manage. But an earlier audit gives the auditor no personal stake in the outcome.
wrong_explanations.B: Past work for a different funder is experience, not responsibility for this activity, and it leaves no interest that competes with the organization's.
wrong_explanations.C: A professional acquaintance is not a close personal relationship or a financial tie. Nothing here gives the auditor a competing interest in the awards.

tips: Eliminate: B, because earlier work for a different funder leaves no stake in these awards, and C, because a professional acquaintance is not a close relationship.
Final two: D beats A because a board seat with an applicant is a competing interest; a past audit of the process is a bias to manage.
Exam cue: a conflict of interest needs a competing interest, such as a role, relationship or investment tied to the outcome. Money is not required.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. Familiarity bias in testing
questions.question: After four clean audits of the same branch, internal auditor Thandi halves the sample and accepts the manager's explanation for two anomalies without checking. What is the GREATEST risk to the engagement?

options.A: Conclusions rest on past impressions instead of current evidence
options.B: The function loses its organizational independence from the branch
options.C: The smaller sample breaches a minimum size set by the Standards
options.D: A conflict of interest arises between Thandi and the manager

questions.key_concept: Familiarity bias lets assumptions from past experience stand in for evidence, which weakens professional skepticism and the support for conclusions.
questions.pre_read: Look at what changed in the auditor's testing, and what that change was based on.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.1 Individual Objectivity requires internal auditors to be aware of their biases and manage them, and its considerations give familiarity bias as an example: assumptions from past experience that weaken professional skepticism. Thandi's smaller sample and unchecked explanations mean this year's conclusions lean on earlier years. A conflict of interest is the runner-up, but nothing shows a competing personal interest; the threat is assumption, not a stake.

wrong_explanations.B: Independence is the function's position, set by its reporting line to the board. One auditor's habits on one branch are a matter of personal objectivity.
wrong_explanations.C: The Standards set no fixed sample size. Information must be relevant, reliable and sufficient; the concern is why the sample shrank, not a numeric minimum.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: long contact can strain objectivity, but a conflict of interest needs a competing interest or close tie. The facts show assumptions from clean results instead.

tips: Eliminate: B, because independence concerns the function's position, not one auditor's habits, and C, because the Standards require sufficient information but set no minimum sample.
Final two: A beats D because nothing shows a competing interest; the danger is past clean results replacing evidence gathered this year.
Exam cue: repeated clean audits followed by lighter testing signal familiarity bias. On CIA questions the harm is weaker skepticism and thinly supported conclusions.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Policies and safeguards for objectivity. Gift during an engagement
questions.question: Midway through an audit of a stadium's ticketing, the ticketing manager offers internal auditor Yusuf two match seats worth less than the organization's gift limit. Which factor should MOST decide whether Yusuf may accept?

options.A: Whether the seats' value is under the organization's gift limit
options.B: Whether the seats count as a tangible item such as cash
options.C: Whether accepting could be presumed to impair Yusuf's objectivity
options.D: Whether Yusuf discloses the seats to the chief audit executive

questions.key_concept: A gift, reward or favor is refused whenever it may impair objectivity or be presumed to; its value and later disclosure do not settle it.
questions.pre_read: Notice who is offering, when, and what the organization's limit does and does not tell you.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity bars internal auditors from accepting any item, tangible or not, that may impair objectivity or be presumed to. Seats offered by the manager of the activity under review, during the engagement, meet that test whatever they cost. Disclosure to the chief audit executive is the runner-up: it makes the offer visible, but it does not turn a gift that looks like influence into one that may be kept.

wrong_explanations.A: The organization's limit is a ceiling for staff in general. The test for an internal auditor is whether objectivity may be impaired, or be presumed to be.
wrong_explanations.B: The rule covers intangible items too, such as hospitality, tickets or a favor. Being tangible or cash is not what makes a gift improper.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: disclosure makes the offer visible, yet it does not cure a gift that could be presumed to influence the auditor's judgment in an ongoing engagement.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the organization's limit does not answer the objectivity test, and B, because intangible items such as hospitality and favors are covered too.
Final two: C beats D because the rule turns on presumed impairment; telling the chief audit executive does not make an influencing gift acceptable.
Exam cue: for gifts, ask how acceptance would look to an outsider. On CIA questions, value limits and disclosure rarely rescue a gift from the audited manager.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Policies and safeguards for objectivity. Assurance over an area the audit head runs
questions.question: A shipyard's chief audit executive also heads risk management, as the charter records, and an assurance engagement on risk management is planned. Which arrangement BEST protects the engagement's objectivity?

options.A: A senior audit manager oversees it and reports to the board
options.B: The chief audit executive oversees it after informing the board
options.C: Risk management staff assess their own function and report the results
options.D: An independent party outside internal audit oversees the engagement

questions.key_concept: Assurance over a function the chief audit executive is responsible for must be overseen by an independent party from outside the internal audit function.
questions.pre_read: Trace the reporting line of each person proposed to oversee the work. Where does it end?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity requires that an assurance engagement over a function the chief audit executive is responsible for be overseen by an independent party from outside the internal audit function. Standard 7.1 Organizational Independence likewise calls for another route to assurance over such a role. A senior audit manager reporting to the board is the runner-up, but that manager still works for the impaired executive every other day.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: reporting this one engagement to the board helps, but the manager is still inside the function and answers to the impaired executive. Oversight must come from outside.
wrong_explanations.B: Telling the board is required, but disclosure does not remove the impairment. The executive would still be overseeing an assessment of their own function.
wrong_explanations.C: A function assessing itself is self-assessment, not independent assurance. It leaves the board with no objective view of risk management.

tips: Eliminate: B, because disclosure to the board does not remove the executive's impairment, and C, because a function's self-assessment is not independent assurance.
Final two: D beats A because everyone inside internal audit answers to the chief audit executive; a party outside the function is free of that tie.
Exam cue: when the chief audit executive runs the area under review, look for oversight from outside internal audit, not a more senior insider.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Policies and safeguards for objectivity. Impairment found after the engagement
questions.question: Two months after a final communication on a payroll provider, a chief audit executive learns that the lead auditor held shares in the provider, though no error has surfaced. What should the executive do FIRST?

options.A: Discuss the concern with the stakeholders it affects
options.B: Reissue the communication without the lead auditor's name
options.C: Have another auditor repeat the work before raising the matter
options.D: Leave the results in place unless an actual error is found

questions.key_concept: An impairment found after an engagement, in fact or appearance, is discussed by the chief audit executive with those affected before the action is determined.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether reliability has to be damaged in fact, or whether looking damaged is enough to act.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.3 Disclosing Impairments to Objectivity covers an impairment discovered after completion that puts the results' reliability in doubt, in fact or in appearance: the chief audit executive must discuss it with the affected parties and determine what to do. Perception alone triggers the duty. Repeating the work first is the runner-up; re-performance may be the agreed action, but it comes after disclosure, not in place of it.

wrong_explanations.B: Removing a name changes nothing about who did the work. Users of the results still would not know that their reliability may be in doubt.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: repeating the work may be the right remedy, but the chief audit executive first discusses the concern with those affected, then determines the action.
wrong_explanations.D: The duty covers perceived reliability as well as actual. Results lose value when users doubt the auditor's objectivity, even with no error found.

tips: Eliminate: B, because removing a name does not tell users about the doubt, and D, because perceived reliability counts even when no error is found.
Final two: A beats C because disclosure and discussion with those affected come first; repeating the work may follow as the action determined.
Exam cue: an impairment discovered late still has to be disclosed. On CIA questions, discuss with the affected parties before choosing or starting the fix.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. Missing technical competency
questions.question: Internal auditor Ines is assigned to lead an assurance engagement on a hospital's radiation-dosing software, a technology nobody in the function understands. What should Ines do FIRST?

options.A: Decline the engagement and ask to remove it from the plan
options.B: Begin fieldwork and build the needed knowledge while testing proceeds
options.C: Raise the gap with the chief audit executive to obtain expertise
options.D: Narrow the scope to the parts the team already understands

questions.key_concept: Internal auditors take on work they have or can obtain the competencies for; a resource gap found in planning goes to the chief audit executive.
questions.pre_read: Before choosing, ask whether a missing skill can be brought in, and who has the means to arrange that.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 3.1 Competency lets internal auditors take on work they can attain the competencies for, and Standard 13.5 Engagement Resources has them raise inappropriate or insufficient resources with the chief audit executive, who can obtain the expertise through training, a guest auditor or an outside provider. Narrowing the scope is the runner-up: it may follow if expertise cannot be found, but it is not the first move.

wrong_explanations.A: A missing skill is not a reason to drop planned work. The competency can be obtained, for example through a specialist, training or an external provider.
wrong_explanations.B: Standard 3.1 limits internal auditors to work they have, or can attain, the competencies for. Starting with no expertise and no plan to get it fails that test.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a reduced scope can result when expertise cannot be obtained, but that comes after the discussion with the chief audit executive, not before it.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a missing competency can be obtained and need not end the engagement, and B, because the work needs competency or a plan to attain it.
Final two: C beats D because the first duty is to raise the resource gap so expertise can be obtained; cutting scope is a later fallback.
Exam cue: when the team lacks a skill, CIA answers usually obtain it, through the chief audit executive, before they decline, improvise or shrink the work.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. Keeping competencies current
questions.question: Internal auditor Rahim, certified for ten years, audits treasury at a bank that is moving to a real-time payments platform Rahim has never reviewed. Which response BEST meets Rahim's professional development duty?

options.A: Rely on the certification as evidence of current competency
options.B: Seek out training on the platform before the engagement
options.C: Wait for the chief audit executive to schedule platform training
options.D: Ask to stay on engagements that match past experience

questions.key_concept: Keeping competencies current is each internal auditor's own responsibility; a certification does not replace learning when the work changes.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns an internal auditor's development, and what a certification earned years ago proves today.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 3.2 Continuing Professional Development requires internal auditors to keep developing their competencies, and Standard 3.1 Competency makes each auditor responsible for doing so. A platform Rahim has never reviewed is a clear signal to act. Waiting for the chief audit executive is the runner-up: the executive must support and encourage development, but the responsibility to pursue it stays with the individual auditor.

wrong_explanations.A: A certification shows competency as it was earned and maintained. It does not cover a technology the auditor has never reviewed.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the chief audit executive supports development through training, feedback and mentoring, but each internal auditor is responsible for pursuing their own.
wrong_explanations.D: Avoiding new subjects lets competencies go stale as the organization changes. The Standards expect internal auditors to keep developing, not to stay with what they know.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a certification does not prove competency in a technology not yet reviewed, and D, because avoiding new areas lets competencies go stale.
Final two: B beats C because each internal auditor owns their development; the chief audit executive supports it but is not the one who must start it.
Exam cue: a new system, law or role signals a development need. On CIA questions the auditor acts on it personally and early.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. Disagreement at the closing meeting
questions.question: At a closing meeting, a wine exporter's logistics head disputes a finding on customs paperwork but offers no new evidence, and discussion brings no agreement. What is the internal auditor's BEST next step?

options.A: Keep the finding and record both positions under the methodology
options.B: Withdraw the finding and keep the working relationship intact
options.C: Lower the finding's rating until both sides accept it
options.D: Repeat the case until the logistics head accepts it

questions.key_concept: When management disagrees, internal auditors seek mutual understanding; without a valid reason the results stand, and both positions are recorded as the methodology provides.
questions.pre_read: Check what the manager brought to the meeting: new facts, or disagreement alone?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.1 Engagement Communication has internal auditors discuss a disagreement and try for a mutual understanding. If none is reached, they need not change the results without a valid reason, and they follow the methodology that lets both sides state their positions. No new evidence means no valid reason. Lowering the rating to win agreement is the runner-up, but a rating follows the evidence, not a bargain.

wrong_explanations.B: Dropping a supported finding to keep the peace leaves out relevant information, which Standard 1.1 forbids. Trust is built on candor, not on silence.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: compromise feels collaborative, but results change for a valid reason such as new evidence. Significance is rated on likelihood and impact, not negotiated.
wrong_explanations.D: Persuasion aims at a shared understanding of the evidence. Once discussion is exhausted, the methodology records both positions; pressing for surrender adds nothing.

tips: Eliminate: B, because withdrawing a supported finding leaves out relevant information, and D, because persuasion seeks understanding of the evidence, not surrender.
Final two: A beats C because results change for a valid reason; with no new evidence, the rating stays and both positions are recorded.
Exam cue: in a disagreement, ask whether management offered new facts. If not, CIA answers keep the results and document both views.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. Cost against benefit
questions.question: A new internal auditor at a tram operator says due professional care means the budget should not limit testing. Which reply from the engagement supervisor is MOST accurate?

options.A: Care means testing until no significant error could remain undetected
options.B: Care applies during fieldwork, once planning has fixed the budget
options.C: Care lets cost set the scope whenever hours are tight
options.D: Care includes weighing the work's cost against its likely benefit

questions.key_concept: Due professional care includes weighing the cost of the work against its potential benefit; it is not a duty to test everything.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether care is about the amount of testing or about the judgment behind it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.2 Due Professional Care lists the cost of the work against its potential benefits among the things an internal auditor must assess, next to the significance of risks and how probable significant errors, fraud and noncompliance are. So budget is weighed, not waved away. Letting cost set the scope is the runner-up, but cost is one factor balanced against benefit and risk, not the deciding one.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal auditors are not expected to be infallible. Care is the diligence and judgment of a prudent, competent auditor, not a promise that nothing is missed.
wrong_explanations.B: Due professional care applies to planning as well as performing. Deciding how much work is needed, and with which techniques, is part of exercising it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: cost does count, but it is weighed against likely benefit and the significance of risks. Tight hours do not justify leaving a significant risk untested.

tips: Eliminate: A, because care is not infallibility or exhaustive testing, and B, because care covers planning as well as performing the work.
Final two: D beats C because cost is weighed against benefit and risk; it informs how much work is worth doing but does not decide alone.
Exam cue: due professional care means proportion. Be wary of options that test everything, and of options that let budget override significant risk.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. Care is not infallibility
questions.question: A regulator fines a credit union over an error in a process its internal auditors reviewed last year. Which question BEST tests whether the internal auditors exercised due professional care?

options.A: Did they examine every transaction in the reviewed process?
options.B: Did they work as a prudent, competent auditor would?
options.C: Did any significant error in the process go undetected?
options.D: Did the process managers agree with the engagement's results?

questions.key_concept: Due professional care is judged by whether the work matched what a prudent, competent internal auditor would do, not by whether every error was caught.
questions.pre_read: Decide whether care is measured by the outcome or by the quality of the planning and the work.
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 4 Exercise Due Professional Care describes care as the diligence, judgment and skepticism of a prudent, competent internal auditor, and adds that infallibility is not expected. So the test is how the work was planned and performed, including how risks were weighed under Standard 4.2. Asking whether an error slipped through is the runner-up, but it judges the outcome, and a careful engagement can still miss something.

wrong_explanations.A: Care weighs cost against benefit and the significance of risks. Examining every transaction is not required, and it would take resources from higher risks.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a missed error invites the question, but internal auditors are not expected to be infallible. Care is judged by the work done, not by the outcome.
wrong_explanations.D: Management's agreement shows acceptance, not quality. Care is measured against a prudent, competent internal auditor's planning and performance.

tips: Eliminate: A, because care does not require testing every transaction, and D, because management's agreement does not measure the quality of the work.
Final two: B beats C because care is judged by how the work was planned and performed; a missed error alone does not prove a lack of care.
Exam cue: after a surprise loss or fine, CIA answers judge due professional care by process and judgment, not by hindsight.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. Corroborating a statement
questions.question: An IT manager at a veterinary group tells internal auditor Sofia that backups are restore-tested every month and offers a summary slide as support. Which response BEST shows professional skepticism?

options.A: Accept the statement and the slide as sufficient support
options.B: Treat the statement as false and report the control as failed
options.C: Inspect the restore-test logs for a sample of recent months
options.D: Ask the manager to confirm the statement in a signed memo

questions.key_concept: Professional skepticism tests whether information is reliable by seeking corroborating evidence, without assuming the person is right or dishonest.
questions.pre_read: For each response, ask where the supporting information would come from.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.3 Professional Skepticism requires internal auditors to assess critically how reliable information is and to seek more evidence where a statement may be incomplete. Standard 14.1 Gathering Information for Analyses and Evaluation adds that information is more reliable when the auditor obtains it directly or corroborates it. Inspecting the logs does that. A signed memo is the runner-up, but it is the same assertion from the same source.

wrong_explanations.A: The statement and the slide come from the same manager, so nothing corroborates either. Skepticism means validating claims with evidence, not taking them on trust.
wrong_explanations.B: Skepticism questions the information, not the person's honesty. Concluding that the control failed, with no testing, is as unsupported as accepting the claim.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a signed memo adds formality, but it repeats the manager's own assertion. Reliability comes from evidence the auditor obtains directly or corroborates.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a statement and a slide from the same manager corroborate nothing, and B, because skepticism doubts the information without presuming the manager is dishonest.
Final two: C beats D because logs the auditor inspects corroborate the claim; a memo repeats the same assertion from the same source.
Exam cue: when told something by management, CIA answers usually corroborate it with evidence obtained directly, neither trusting nor accusing.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. Ownership of workpapers
questions.question: Internal auditor Tane is leaving a dental chain and wants to keep copies of engagement workpapers as samples for job interviews. What is the BEST course of action?

options.A: Keep copies of the workpapers that Tane personally prepared
options.B: Keep copies after removing names and account numbers
options.C: Ask the managers of the audited areas to approve the copies
options.D: Leave every copy in the internal audit function's custody

questions.key_concept: Engagement information stays the organization's; an internal auditor uses it for professional purposes and leaves records in the function's custody.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns the information in a workpaper, and what purpose the planned use would serve.
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 5 Maintain Confidentiality has internal auditors respect the ownership of information and use it for professional purposes, and Standard 5.1 Use of Information bars using it for personal gain. Standard 5.2 Protection of Information puts custody and retention of engagement records under the function's rules. Removing names is the runner-up: it eases the privacy concern, but the records are still the organization's and the use is still personal.

wrong_explanations.A: Preparing a workpaper does not make the auditor its owner. The information was obtained for the organization's audit work and remains the organization's.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: removing names protects individuals, but the content is still proprietary and the purpose is still personal benefit, not professional use.
wrong_explanations.C: Managers of an audited area do not control engagement records. Custody, retention and release follow the internal audit function's methodologies.

tips: Eliminate: A, because writing a workpaper does not transfer ownership to the auditor, and C, because audited managers do not control the function's records.
Final two: D beats B because redaction addresses privacy alone; ownership and the bar on personal use still apply to what remains.
Exam cue: access is not ownership. On CIA questions, engagement information serves the engagement and stays under the function's custody rules.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. Privacy rules and audit access
questions.question: Internal auditor Greta wants to copy a physiotherapy chain's billing data to a personal analytics tool, citing the charter's unrestricted access, although policy keeps personal data in an approved environment. Which action is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Copy the data, relying on the charter's unrestricted access
options.B: Analyze the data inside the approved environment the policy requires
options.C: Copy the data after removing the patients' names and addresses
options.D: Drop the billing tests that would need the patients' data

questions.key_concept: Unrestricted access lets internal auditors obtain information; laws, regulations and policies still govern how they use, move and store it.
questions.pre_read: Separate two questions: may the auditor see the data, and how must the data be handled once seen?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 5.1 Use of Information requires internal auditors to use information as the applicable laws, regulations, policies and procedures direct, and Standard 5.2 Protection of Information adds those on privacy and information security. The charter grants access; it does not waive the handling rules. Removing names is the runner-up: it lowers the exposure, but the data would still leave the approved environment that the policy requires.

wrong_explanations.A: Access under the charter answers whether the auditor may see the data. Handling it is still governed by privacy law and the organization's policies.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: masking names reduces exposure, but billing records can still identify people, and the policy's approved environment would still be bypassed.
wrong_explanations.D: Sensitivity is managed with protection, not avoidance. Internal auditors have access to do the work and then handle the data as policy requires.

tips: Eliminate: A, because access under the charter does not waive privacy and handling rules, and D, because sensitive data is protected, not left untested.
Final two: B beats C because the policy requires the approved environment; stripping names lowers the risk but still moves personal data outside it.
Exam cue: the mandate gives access; law and policy govern use. On CIA questions the auditor does the work inside the handling rules.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. Request from a senior colleague
questions.question: After an engagement on a confidential plant closure plan, internal auditor Bashir is asked by a sales director outside the project which plant will close. Which response is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Decline, and explain that the plan is limited to authorized people
options.B: Decline, and state that the engagement did not cover plant closures
options.C: Answer verbally and keep the written workpapers restricted
options.D: Answer once the director promises to keep it confidential

questions.key_concept: Confidential information goes to people authorized to receive it; seniority, a promise of secrecy or a spoken answer does not create authorization.
questions.pre_read: Ask what would make this person entitled to the answer: rank, a promise, or something else?
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 5 Maintain Confidentiality protects information from unauthorized disclosure inside the organization as well as outside, and Standard 5.2 Protection of Information bars disclosure to unauthorized parties unless a legal or professional responsibility applies. A director outside the project is not authorized, so Bashir declines, honestly. Answering once secrecy is promised is the runner-up, but a promise does not make the director an authorized recipient.

wrong_explanations.B: Confidentiality does not permit a false statement. Standard 1.1 requires internal auditors to be truthful, so the right refusal is an honest one.
wrong_explanations.C: The duty covers information passed on in conversation as well as in documents. Telling the director aloud is still an unauthorized disclosure.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a promise limits further spread, but authorization comes from the organization's rules, not from the requester's rank or assurances.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a refusal must still be truthful, and C, because spoken disclosure is covered by the confidentiality duty as much as written.
Final two: A beats D because authorization, not rank or a promise of secrecy, decides who may receive confidential information.
Exam cue: for any request for engagement information, ask one question first: is this person authorized to have it? Employment and seniority do not answer it.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. Lawful demand for workpapers
questions.question: A regulator's lawful order for mine safety workpapers reaches internal auditor Dao, whose function routes outside releases through the chief audit executive; the operations director urges refusal on confidentiality grounds. What should Dao do FIRST?

options.A: Refuse the order and cite the confidentiality of engagement records
options.B: Send the full workpapers to the regulator straight away
options.C: Refer the order to the chief audit executive
options.D: Let the operations director decide what is released

questions.key_concept: A legal duty to disclose overrides confidentiality, but the release still follows the function's route, through the chief audit executive.
questions.pre_read: Two questions are mixed here: whether the records may be released, and who handles the release.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 5.2 Protection of Information bars disclosure to unauthorized parties unless a legal or professional responsibility requires it, and Standard 1.3 Legal and Ethical Behavior has internal auditors make the disclosures the law requires. So refusal is wrong. Standard 5.2 also places the release of engagement records under the function's rules, which here run through the chief audit executive. Sending everything at once is the runner-up: lawful in aim, but it bypasses that route.

wrong_explanations.A: The confidentiality duty carries an exception for legal responsibility, and internal auditors must make the disclosures that laws and regulations require.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the order must be met, but engagement records are released under the function's methodology, here through the chief audit executive, who can take legal advice first.
wrong_explanations.D: Managers of the activity under review do not control the internal audit function's records or decide how a lawful order is answered.

tips: Eliminate: A, because confidentiality yields to a legal duty to disclose, and D, because audited management does not control the function's records.
Final two: C beats B because the release must follow the function's route; the chief audit executive handles it and can take legal advice first.
Exam cue: on outside requests for audit records, CIA answers neither refuse a lawful demand nor release alone. They route it through the chief audit executive.
